title: The Impact of Air Pollution on Infant Mortality: Evidence from Geographic Variation in Pollution Shocks Induced by a Recession
research_question: Does exposure to particulate air pollution causally affect infant mortality and birth outcomes, and if so, through what stage of development (fetal versus postnatal) does this effect operate? Are there nonlinearities or thresholds in the pollution–infant health relationship, and do effects differ by race and gender?
data_description: The study merges multiple comprehensive U.S. datasets covering 1978–1984 at the county-year level. Infant deaths come from the annual National Mortality Detail Files (universe of death certificates), providing age at death, cause (internal vs. external), race, gender, and county of residence. Births come from the National Natality Detail Files (universe of birth certificates), providing parental demographics, prenatal care, maternal medical history, gestational age, birth weight, APGAR scores, and congenital conditions. Air pollution data are total suspended particulates (TSPs) annual geometric means from roughly 4,000 EPA monitors (Quick Look Report from the AQS database) for ~1,200 counties/year. Additional county-level data include BEA per-capita income, BLS unemployment rates, REIS transfer payments (Medicaid, Medicare, AFDC, Food Stamps, SSI, UI), County Business Patterns manufacturing employment, 1983 County and City Data Book characteristics (demographics, crime, medical providers, fiscal variables), state-level Medicaid data, and National Weather Service temperature/precipitation. The unit of observation is the county-year (with race-gender cells available).
institutional_context: The setting is the sharp 1981–82 U.S. recession, which generated unusually large and geographically uneven reductions in particulate air pollution. Heavily industrialized counties—particularly those with steel and other pollution-intensive manufacturing such as Pittsburgh, PA—experienced dramatic plant shutdowns and consequent steep declines in TSPs, while neighboring counties also benefited via cross-boundary air transport. Counties without pollution-intensive industry and not adjacent to such areas saw little change. Nationally, average TSPs fell over 20% in just two years, a decline as large as the cumulative improvement following the 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments. Plant closures during this episode were largely permanent because reopenings and new investments fell under the stricter 1977 CAAA, which required state-of-the-art abatement technology and pollution offsets. The EPA also enforced a 75 µg/m³ annual TSP attainment ceiling at the county level, making knowledge of potential thresholds in pollution’s health effects directly policy-relevant. This episode produced abrupt, geographically heterogeneous pollution shocks within a narrow window, while other determinants of infant health changed little.
